To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the performance of Time Warp can be significantly improved by canceling back more memory objects than the number of events that have to be rolled back, and (2) a small amount of additional memory can be used to achieve a performance nearly equivalent to the one with large amounts of additional memory, if the memory management overhead is small compared to the granularity of the events.

the memory requirements of the Time Warp simulation mechanism can be controlled to a large extent without any significant loss in performance, and that the speedup-memory curve for Time Warp simulations exhibits a well-defined knee, beyond which the performance gain with additional memory becomes insignificant.
(1) Time Warp can be used with a small amount of memory and (2) a small amount of additional memory can improve performance significantly.
In summary, our research is concerned with
evaluating the performance of a distributed simulation system when memory resources are constrained.
the development of a memory management strategy for Time Warp that can be used in a wide variety of parallel architectures and applications.
understanding the behavior of Time Warps with respect to memory requirements.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the performance vs. limited memory tradeoff in Time Warp is not as bad as it is commonly perceived to be.
the performance-memory tradeoff for Time Warp depends on the workload, the amount of memory available, and the overheads incurred by the memory management protocol.

the performance of Time Warp can be made to scale well even with a limited memory, but that the amount of memory required is a strong function of the event granularity, the asymmetry of the workload, and the memory management overhead.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
a Time Warp implementation can be tuned to run with very little memory and still achieve a performance close to that of an implementation with large memory, if memory management is done carefully.
the cancelback protocol provides a simple and efficient solution to the memory management problem in Time Warp.
the Time Warp mechanism can be implemented in a manner that is efficient in both memory usage and performance.
The main takeaway from our work is that
Time Warp programs can be made more memory-efficient without sacrificing performance.
Time Warp can be made to work well even with limited memory.

the performance of Time Warp under memory constraints is not as bad as is generally thought to be, and that the performance-memory tradeoff can be effectively controlled by judicious use of the cancelback mechanism.
